In this guide, I'll walk you through everything you need to configure MCP servers in Gemini CLI. From basic setup to advanced configurations with tools like BrainGrid.

#What is a Gemini CLI MCP Server?

A Gemini CLI MCP server is a bridge between Google's Gemini CLI and external services. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives Gemini context beyond your local files. Think databases, APIs, cloud services, and project specifications.

When you connect a database MCP server to Gemini CLI, it can examine your actual tables and columns. The SQL it generates uses real schema names, not placeholders. When you connect BrainGrid MCP, Gemini reads your requirements and acceptance criteria directly, building features that match your specifications.

What Gemini CLI MCP servers enable:

  • Query live database schemas
  • Fetch real API responses
  • Read structured specifications from BrainGrid
  • Access GitHub issues, PRs, and commit history
  • Connect to cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP)

Here's how the flow works:

Loading diagram...

MCP transforms Gemini from a code generator into a context-aware development partner.

#Why Gemini CLI MCP Servers Matter for Developers

Without MCP servers, every Gemini CLI session starts from scratch. You paste schemas, explain API structures, and fix the same boilerplate over and over. That copy-paste cycle kills momentum.

With Gemini CLI MCP servers configured:

  • Database queries use your actual schema
  • API code handles real response formats
  • Specifications stay consistent across sessions
  • Less manual fixing, faster shipping

The pattern applies across your entire stack. A GitHub MCP server gives Gemini context about open issues. A Stripe MCP server lets it understand billing flows. BrainGrid MCP provides structured requirements instead of vague prompts.

When Gemini has direct access to your systems, the code it generates works the first time.

#How to Set Up Gemini CLI MCP Servers

Gemini CLI supports MCP server configuration through two methods. You can use CLI commands for quick setup, or JSON configuration files for persistent settings.

#Adding Gemini MCP Servers via CLI

The gemini mcp add command configures MCP servers without editing files manually.

Add a remote HTTP MCP server (like BrainGrid):

1gemini mcp add --transport http braingrid https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp

Add a remote SSE MCP server:

1gemini mcp add --transport sse my-sse-server https://api.example.com/sse

Add a local stdio MCP server:

1gemini mcp add my-local-server python server.py -- --port 8080

The -- separates Gemini CLI flags from arguments passed to the MCP server process.

Add MCP server with environment variables:

1gemini mcp add -e GITHUB_TOKEN=$GITHUB_TOKEN github npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github

Add MCP server with custom headers:

1gemini mcp add --transport http --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" my-api https://api.example.com/mcp

By default, Gemini CLI adds MCP servers to the project config (.gemini/settings.json). Use -s user to add to user config (~/.gemini/settings.json) instead.

#Configuring Gemini MCP Servers in settings.json

For persistent Gemini CLI MCP configuration, edit your settings.json file directly.

Gemini CLI MCP config file locations:

  • User config: ~/.gemini/settings.json
  • Project config: .gemini/settings.json

Here's an example settings.json with multiple MCP servers configured:

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "braingrid": {
4      "httpUrl": "https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp"
5    },
6    "github": {
7      "command": "npx",
8      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
9      "env": {
10        "GITHUB_TOKEN": "$GITHUB_TOKEN"
11      }
12    },
13    "postgres": {
14      "command": "npx",
15      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres"],
16      "env": {
17        "DATABASE_URL": "$DATABASE_URL"
18      }
19    }
20  }
21}

#Gemini CLI MCP Server Configuration Format

Each MCP server entry uses specific properties that determine how Gemini CLI connects.

Transport is determined by property name:

  • httpUrl for HTTP streaming transport (remote hosted MCP servers)
  • url for SSE transport (Server-Sent Events MCP servers)
  • command for Stdio transport (local subprocess MCP servers)
Loading diagram...

Gemini CLI MCP configuration properties:

PropertyDescription
httpUrlHTTP streaming endpoint URL for remote MCP servers
urlSSE endpoint URL for Server-Sent Events MCP servers
commandExecutable path for local MCP servers
argsArguments passed to the MCP server command
envEnvironment variables ($VAR or ${VAR} syntax)
headersCustom HTTP headers for remote MCP servers
cwdWorking directory for local MCP servers
timeoutRequest timeout in milliseconds (default: 600,000)
trustSkip confirmation prompts when true
includeToolsAllowlist of MCP tool names to enable
excludeToolsBlocklist of MCP tool names to disable

Example Gemini MCP server with headers and timeout:

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "authenticated-api": {
4      "httpUrl": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
5      "headers": {
6        "Authorization": "Bearer $API_TOKEN",
7        "X-Custom-Header": "value"
8      },
9      "timeout": 30000
10    }
11  }
12}

#Managing Gemini CLI MCP Servers

List all configured MCP servers:

1gemini mcp list

Remove an MCP server:

1gemini mcp remove braingrid

Disable MCP server temporarily:

1gemini mcp disable braingrid
2gemini mcp enable braingrid

Check MCP server status inside Gemini CLI:

This displays connection status, available tools, and any errors for each configured MCP server.

Here are the MCP servers I find most useful with Gemini CLI:

  • Database MCP servers: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Supabase, Neon. Gemini queries schemas, understands relationships, and generates accurate SQL.

  • GitHub MCP server: Read PRs, inspect issues, understand commit history. Repository context that influences code but doesn't live in local files.

#BrainGrid MCP Server: Spec-Driven Development in Gemini CLI

BrainGrid is an AI product manager that helps developers plan, specify, and build features. I've noticed most developers (myself included) jump straight into prompting before having a clear picture of what we're building. Running initial ideas through BrainGrid turns them into structured requirements.

Say you want to add user authentication. BrainGrid analyzes your codebase and asks clarifying questions. Which auth providers? What session handling? How to manage password resets? #Troubleshooting Gemini CLI MCP Server Issues

MCP server shows DISCONNECTED: Check the URL for typos. Test connectivity with curl https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp. VPNs and firewalls can block MCP traffic.

OAuth popup doesn't appear: Gemini CLI MCP OAuth requires a local browser. It won't work in headless servers or SSH sessions. Authenticate on a machine with a browser, then copy ~/.gemini/mcp-oauth-tokens.json to the target machine.

MCP tools not showing up: Run /mcp to check connection status. Verify includeTools isn't filtering them out. Complete OAuth authorization if required.

MCP server timeout errors: Increase the timeout in your Gemini CLI MCP configuration:

1{

6    }
7  }
8}

Stdio MCP server won't start on Windows: Wrap commands with cmd:

1{

3    "windows-server": {
4      "command": "cmd",
5      "args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "my-mcp-server"]
6    }
7  }
8}

Changes not taking effect: Restart Gemini CLI after modifying settings.json or adding new MCP servers.

title: The Difference Between Writing Software and Shipping Software
subtitle: AI agents write code faster than ever, but most still have no idea what happens after it deploys. Here's why the next big leap in AI engineering is observation, not smarter code.
content:
A few years ago, getting AI to write code felt almost impossible. Today it feels completely normal, almost boring in a good way.

AI agents can build React apps, scaffold APIs, and help refactor entire codebases. They can even help explain previously unknown codebases. What used to take hours, can now be done in minutes. It has indisputably gotten much better.

Thanks for reading No One Told You This! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

But over the past few months I’ve noticed something. Every time an AI agent proudly tells me “done,” in my head I’m immediately like, girl, is it tho?

Because writing software and shipping software are not the same thing, no matter how confident that little “done” message sounds. Code is only one part of the job. After the last line is written, there’s a whole messy world still waiting on the other side of it: deploying the app, connecting a database, managing secrets, reading logs when something breaks at the worst possible time, restarting a service that crashed for no reason, actually verifying that any of it works instead of just believing it does. This is the point where software stops being text on a screen and starts becoming something real, with real consequences if it’s wrong. And right now, that’s usually exactly where AI checks out.

How we got here…

If you look at how AI coding tools have evolved, it’s honestly a pretty fun arc to trace. We started with autocomplete, basically fancy autocorrect for developers. Then came chat inside the IDE, which felt like magic at the time. Then agents that could edit multiple files, run terminal commands, and reason across an entire repo, which felt like actual magic. More recently, agents have started reaching outward through protocols like MCP, calling external tools and acting with way more autonomy than before.

Every step gave AI more room to work in, and every step got a “wow” out of me. But the world it actually understood stayed roughly the same the whole time. It was still mostly the codebase. The infrastructure underneath it, the place where the software actually lives and runs and occasionally sets itself on fire, stayed invisible.

That’s why an agent can tell you with total confidence that a deployment should work, while the container is quietly crashing because of one missing environment variable it never even knew existed. Or tell you a migration succeeded while the database never actually started. The AI isn’t lying to you, it’s not even wrong exactly, it just can’t see what’s happening on the other side of the screen. It’s making calls with half the information and reporting back like it has all of it.

The question that actually matters now

I think that’s where the next real shift is going to happen. For the last couple of years the question everyone’s been asking is how do we make AI better at writing code. Honestly? I think the more interesting question now is how do we let AI actually operate the systems it helps build.

Those are two very different problems. Writing code is prediction. Operating software is observation, and observation needs feedback, no way around it. You need logs, you need deployment status, you need to know the exact moment something broke and why. Without that loop, AI is basically guessing at what happened after the code left the editor, and then telling you it’s fine with a straight face.

What I’ve been seeing up close

I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately because it’s something I run into in my actual day to day work, not just as a hot take I saw online. One of the things I’ve been spending time at Zerops where I currently work is called ZCP, and what’s interesting about it isn’t that it makes the AI smarter, because honestly, it doesn’t really. What it does is give the AI access to something it usually never gets: the actual environment the software runs in. So instead of stopping the second it generates code, it can watch a deployment happen in real time, read the real logs, understand the project’s infrastructure, and actually check whether what it just did worked, instead of just assuming it did and moving on with its life.

Honestly, the tool itself isn’t even the most interesting part to me. It’s the direction it’s pointing toward. I don’t think the future belongs to AI that just writes better code, I think it belongs to AI that can close the loop completely, start to finish, no vibes-based guessing in between.

Picture an agent that doesn’t stop the moment it opens a pull request. It deploys the app, notices the deployment failed, reads the logs, figures out what actually went wrong, fixes the config, deploys again, and only then says done, and actually means it this time. That’s a fundamentally different kind of assistant. Not because it writes better code, but because it’s finally connected to what’s real.

The actual takeaway

Maybe that’s the next real evolution in AI engineering. Not a bigger model, not a longer context window, not another benchmark flex. Just better feedback, the unglamorous kind nobody puts in a keynote.

Because we don’t become better engineers by writing more code, we become better engineers by seeing what actually happens after we ship it and dealing with it when it’s 3am and something’s on fire. Maybe it’s time our AI agents learned that same lesson too.

title: No One Told Me How to Do This, So I'm Telling You Instead
subtitle: An engineering degree, a global pandemic, and the accidental discovery of a career called DevRel.
content:
Hi, I’m Vanshika!

I know a lot of people end up in tech because it feels like the safe bet, the easiest way to a stable paycheck in this economy. That was never really my story. When people used to ask little kid me what I wanted to be, I would say software engineer without blinking. I was the kid who would grab someone’s phone just to poke around and see how it worked, the kid who would look at some random platform and think this is so cool. I still remember running my first program on Turbo C++ and feeling a kind of happiness I genuinely can’t describe, and honestly, that feeling never really left.

So when I graduated in 2022 with an engineering degree, the plan seemed obvious. Study hard, clear the placement exams, get a corporate job, become a software engineer, and go to office every day. That was the script everyone around me was running, and I figured I would run it too.

Then COVID hit, and that plan got interrupted in a way that turned out to be a an amazing thing.

Stuck at home with a lot of time and a laptop, I stumbled onto Twitter, and not the doomscrolling kind but the actual builder community, full of people shipping things, talking about products, and talking to the people building them. Somewhere in there, I found out about a role I had never even heard of in college, something called DevRel.

Here is the thing about me. I was a quiet kid, genuinely quiet, and yet somehow I always felt strangely comfortable on stage. Before going up, I would have a full blown panic attack, complete with sweaty hands and all the nervous energy you can imagine. But the second I was actually up there, something would just flow naturally, almost like a switch had been flipped. My first keynote was exactly like that. I was terrified backstage and then completely fine the moment I started talking.

For a long time I assumed that contradiction meant DevRel was not really for me, since I am an introvert and it never quite made sense how that could work. But I have come to realize it was never really about being a social person in the traditional sense. I still don’t know what to call the specific kind of person I am, but what I do know is that I genuinely love talking to new people and understanding how they see the world. That curiosity is really the whole thing that makes this work for me, since it was never about performing on stage but about being genuinely interested in someone else’s perspective.

That same curiosity, combined with an instinct I have always had for writing simply, without unnecessary complexity or jargon, is what I have built four plus years of a DevRel career on, working across AI and developer tooling the entire time.

So what is this newsletter?

No One Told You This is going to be the home for everything I have picked up along the way, especially the stuff that never shows up in an onboarding doc or a polished LinkedIn post. You can expect three kinds of posts from me going forward.

Honest takes on new AI tools, since I try things early, before they get saturated, and tell you what actually works and what is just noise.

What DevRel life actually looks like, including the community building, the content, and all the unglamorous parts of making developers genuinely care about a product.

The career stuff no one puts in a job post, especially what it is really like to build a career in a role that did not even have a name when I was still in college.

Why “No One Told You This”?

Because it is literally true. No one told me any of this while I was figuring it out, not how DevRel actually worked, not how to build a career in something that barely existed yet, and not how to be an introvert who somehow feels fine the moment she steps on stage. I had to learn all of it by doing it, often badly, mostly in public, and by asking a lot of questions along the way.

So this is me telling you instead. I am going to try to keep it fun, and I am going to keep it honest, since that is really the only rule I hold myself to in anything I create.

Expect a lot from me, and let’s go.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

title: Build a Telegram Bot to Send Money to US ACH bank Accounts
subtitle: Build a Telegram bot that triggers ACH transfers on agent rails
content:
Tired of that whole dance of asking for account numbers, bank details, and “wait, did you send it yet?”

Yeah, me too!

So I built something better — a Telegram bot that lets anyone send and receive bank payments using just your phone number. No app installs. No awkward copy-paste. Just chat → money moved.

Check out the video here!

In this post, I’ll walk you through how I built it using Node.js, Telegram’s API, and a neat AI Agent payments layer called PaymanAI.

Let’s build it, step-by-step.

What You’ll Need

Before we start, make sure you have a few things ready:

  • A Telegram account (duh — you’ll need this to create the bot)
  • A PaymanAI account with client credentials (sign up here)
  • Node.js (v20 or higher recommended)
  • ngrok (to make your local bot publicly accessible for Telegram)

Step 1: Create Your Telegram Bot

First things first, we need a bot. Telegram makes this super easy.

  1. Open Telegram and search for a user called @BotFather .

2. Start a chat with him and type /newbot.

3. It’ll ask for a name for your bot (like “PayACH Bot”) and a username (which must end in `bot`, like `payach_bot`).

4. Once you’re done, BotFather will give you a token. This token is your bot’s password — keep it safe! We’ll need it in a moment.

Step 2: Set Up Your Project

Now, let’s get our coding environment ready. Open up your terminal and follow along.

1. Create a project folder:

mkdir payach-bot
cd payach-bot

2. Initialize a Node.js project:

npm init -y

This creates a package.json file, which will keep track of our project’s details and dependencies.

3. Install the necessary libraries:

We need a few tools to build our bot:

  • express: A web server framework to receive messages from Telegram.
  • axios: To send messages back to the Telegram API.
  • dotenv: To manage our secret keys (like that bot token).
  • @paymanai/payman-ts: The official SDK for our payment processor.

Run this command to install them all:

npm install express axios dotenv @paymanai/payman-ts

4. Create your main file:

This is where all our bot’s logic will live.

touch index.js

5. Create a `.env` file for your secrets:

This is super important for security. Never write your secret keys directly in your code!

touch .env

Now, open this new .env file and add your keys. It should look like this (replace the placeholder values with your actual keys):

# Telegram Bot Token from BotFather
TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=your-telegram-token-from-botfather

# Your PaymanAI credentials
PAYMAN_CLIENT_ID=your-payman-client-id
PAYMAN_CLIENT_SECRET=your-payman-client-secret

# The port your server will run on
PORT=3000

Step 3: Writing the Bot’s Code

This is the fun part! Open up your index.js file and let’s start coding. We’ll build this up piece by piece.

This bot:

  • Verifies a user’s phone number
  • Links their account + routing number
  • Lets someone else send money to that phone
  • Uses PaymanAI under the hood to move the money
require("dotenv").config();
const express = require("express");
const axios = require("axios");
const { PaymanClient } = require("@paymanai/payman-ts");

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// Telegram & Payman config
const TG_API = `https://api.telegram.org/bot${process.env.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}`;
const payman = PaymanClient.withCredentials({
  clientId: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_ID,
  clientSecret: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_SECRET,
});

// In-memory store (quick and dirty for now)
const usersByPhone = new Map();       // phone → { telegramId, name, ach: {account, routing} }
const phoneByUserId = new Map();      // telegramId → phone
const userContext = new Map();        // telegramId → lastTargetPhone

// Helpers
function normalizePhone(input) {
  return input.replace(/\D/g, "").replace(/^91/, "");
}

function send(chatId, text, kb) {
  return axios.post(`${TG_API}/sendMessage`, {
    chat_id: chatId,
    text,
    parse_mode: "Markdown",
    reply_markup: kb
      ? { keyboard: kb, one_time_keyboard: true, resize_keyboard: true }
      : undefined,
  });
}

// Webhook handler
app.post("/webhook", async (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(200);
  const m = req.body.message;
  if (!m) return;

  const { chat, from, text, contact } = m;
  const chatId = chat.id;
  const userId = from.id;

  try {
    // Contact shared (after /setup)
    if (contact) {
      if (contact.user_id !== userId)
        return send(chatId, "Please share *your own* contact.");

      const phone = normalizePhone(contact.phone_number);
      usersByPhone.set(phone, {
        telegramId: userId,
        name: contact.first_name || "Payee",
        ach: {},
      });
      phoneByUserId.set(userId, phone);

      return send(
        chatId,
        `✅ Phone verified!

Now add your account details:
/account <number>`
      );
    }

    if (!text) return;

    // /start
    if (text === "/start") {
      return send(
        chatId,
        `👋 *Welcome to PayACH!*
Send and receive money using just a phone number.

Start with /setup to link your phone.`
      );
    }

    // /help
    if (text === "/help") {
      return send(
        chatId,
        `📖 *Help Menu*

/setup — Link your phone number
/account 123456 — Add your bank account
/routing 001234567 — Add routing number

To pay: Send a phone number, then \`send $AMOUNT\``
      );
    }

    // /setup
    if (text === "/setup") {
      return send(
        chatId,
        "Tap below to verify your phone.",
        [[{ text: "📞 Verify My Phone", request_contact: true }]]
      );
    }

    // /account
    if (text.startsWith("/account")) {
      const phone = phoneByUserId.get(userId);
      if (!phone) return send(chatId, "⚠️ Use /setup first.");
      const user = usersByPhone.get(phone);

      const account = text.split(" ")[1];
      if (!/^\d+$/.test(account))
        return send(chatId, "❌ Invalid account number.");

      user.ach.account = account;
      return send(chatId, "✅ Account saved. Now add routing via `/routing <number>`");
    }

    // /routing
    if (text.startsWith("/routing")) {
      const phone = phoneByUserId.get(userId);
      if (!phone) return send(chatId, "⚠️ Use /setup first.");
      const user = usersByPhone.get(phone);
      if (!user.ach.account)
        return send(chatId, "Please add your account number first.");

      const routing = text.split(" ")[1];
      if (!/^\d{9}$/.test(routing))
        return send(chatId, "❌ Routing number must be 9 digits.");

      user.ach.routing = routing;
      return send(chatId, "🎉 You’re all set to receive ACH payments!");
    }

    // Phone number lookup
    if (/^\+?\d[\d\s-]{8,}\d$/.test(text)) {
      const phone = normalizePhone(text);
      const recipient = usersByPhone.get(phone);

      if (!recipient?.ach?.account || !recipient?.ach?.routing)
        return send(chatId, "❌ This number isn’t linked to any account yet.");

      userContext.set(userId, { lastTargetPhone: phone });
      return send(
        chatId,
        `✅ Found *${recipient.name}*.
To pay, type: \`send $50\``
      );
    }

    // send $AMOUNT
    if (/^send \$\d+(\.\d+)?$/i.test(text)) {
      const context = userContext.get(userId);
      if (!context?.lastTargetPhone)
        return send(chatId, "Who are you trying to pay? Send their phone number first.");

      const recipient = usersByPhone.get(context.lastTargetPhone);
      const amount = parseFloat(text.match(/\$(\d+(\.\d+)?)/)[1]);

      try {
        await payman.ask(
          `Send $${amount} via ACH to ${recipient.name} (${recipient.ach.account}, ${recipient.ach.routing})`,
          {
            metadata: {
              source: "Telegram Bot",
              phone: context.lastTargetPhone,
            },
          }
        );
        userContext.delete(userId);
        return send(chatId, `💸 Sent *$${amount}* to *${recipient.name}*.`);
      } catch (err) {
        console.error(err);
        return send(chatId, "❌ Payment failed. Check logs for more info.");
      }
    }

    // fallback
    return send(chatId, "🤔 Not sure what that means. Try /help.");
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("Unhandled error:", err);
    return send(chatId, "Something broke. Please try again later.");
  }
});

// Start server
app.listen(process.env.PORT, () =>
  console.log(`✅ PayACH bot running at http://localhost:${process.env.PORT}`)
);

Step 4: Running the Bot and Connecting to Telegram

We have our code. Now, let’s bring it to life.

1. Start your local server:

In your terminal, run:

node index.js

You should see the message: ✅ PayACH bot running at http://localhost:3000

2. Expose your server with ngrok:

Your bot is running on your machine, but Telegram needs a public URL to talk to it. That’s where ngrok comes in.

- Open a new terminal window.

- Run the following command. Make sure to use the same port from your .env file (e.g., 3000).

ngrok http 3000
ngrok will give you a public Forwarding URL that looks like https://random-string.ngrok-free.app Copy this HTTPS URL.

3. Set the Telegram Webhook:

The final step is to tell Telegram where to send messages.

Run this curl command in your terminal.

Remember to replace <YOUR_NGROK_URL> with the URL you just copied from ngrok.
curl "https://api.telegram.org/bot${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/setWebhook?url=<YOUR_NGROK_URL>/webhook"

You should get a response like {"ok":true, "result": true, "description": "Webhook was set"}

Important Note: Every time you restart ngrok, you get a new public URL. You will have to run the curl command again with the new URL.

You’re All Set!

That’s it! Your bot is now live. Open Telegram, find your bot, and start a conversation. You can go through the entire flow: /setup , add your details, and then (from another account) try sending yourself a payment.

Happy Hacking!

Build a Telegram Bot to Send Money to US ACH bank Accounts was originally published in Payman AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Build a Slack Payment AI Agent to Send Money Instantly
subtitle: Build a Slack AI agent that processes payments through API integration
content:
We’ve been building AI systems that can reason, follow instructions, and take action. But the magic really starts when those systems can move money — instantly, securely, and contextually.

So we asked: “What if we could send money… without leaving Slack?”

Turns out, we can!

We built a Slack bot that lets anyone at Payman create payees and send payments , just by typing:

/pay $500 to Sarah
/create crypto John john@company.com 0x123...abc ethereum

No UI. No dashboards. Just Slack. Let’s build it.

Prerequisites

  • A Slack workspace where you can install custom apps
  • A PaymanAI account with client credentials (sign up here)
  • Node.js 18+
  • ngrok (for local development)

Step 1: Set Up the Project

Let’s start with a fresh Next.js project and install Payman SDK

npx create-next-app@latest slack-payment-bot --typescript --tailwind --app
cd slack-payment-bot
npm install @paymanai/payman-ts

Create a .env.localfile:

PAYMAN_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id
PAYMAN_CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret
To get your client credentials and setup Payman, check the docs here.

Then:

npm run dev
npx ngrok http 3000

Copy the HTTPS URL ngrok gives you. This is what you’ll use to connect your Slack app.

Step 2: Create a Slack App

  1. Go to api.slack.com/apps
  2. Click Create New App → From scratch
  3. Give it a name (like “Payman Bot”) and pick your workspace

Add Slash Commands

In your Slack app settings:

  1. Go to Slash Commands → Create New Command
  2. Add:
    - Command: /create
    - Request URL:     https://your-ngrok-url.ngrok.io/api/slack/create
    - Short Description:     Create a new payee
  3. Then another:
    - Command: /pay
    - Request URL:     https://your-ngrok-url.ngrok.io/api/slack/pay
    - Short Description:     Send a payment
  4. Click Save

Add Scopes

Under OAuth & Permissions, add the following scopes:

  • commands
  • chat:write

Then click Install to Workspace.

Step 3 : Adding the Logic

We’ll create two API routes in the Next.js app:

app/api/slack/create/route.ts  ← handles /create
app/api/slack/pay/route.ts     ← handles /pay

Both routes use the Payman TS SDK and Slack’s response_url to handle async replies.

1. Create Payee Logic

app/api/slack/create/route.ts

 import { PaymanClient } from "@paymanai/payman-ts";

// Parse payee names from PaymanAI response content
function parsePayeeNames(payeesContent: string): string[] {
  return payeesContent
    .split("
")
    .map(line => line.match(/^\s*(?:\d+\.|\•)\s*([^(]+?)(?:\s*\([^)]*\))?\s*$/))
    .filter(Boolean)
    .map(match => match![1].trim());
}

// Find case-insensitive match for a payee name
function findPayeeMatch(payeeNames: string[], targetName: string): string | null {
  const target = targetName.toLowerCase().trim();
  return payeeNames.find(name => name.toLowerCase().trim() === target) || null;
}

// Parse quoted and unquoted arguments from a Slack command
function parseQuotedArgs(text: string): string[] {
  const args: string[] = [];
  let current = "";
  let inQuotes = false;

  for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
    const char = text[i];
    if (char === '"') {
      inQuotes = !inQuotes;
    } else if (char === " " && !inQuotes) {
      if (current.trim()) {
        args.push(current.trim());
        current = "";
      }
    } else {
      current += char;
    }
  }

  if (current.trim()) args.push(current.trim());
  return args;
}

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const formData = await req.formData();
  const text = formData.get("text") as string;
  const responseUrl = formData.get("response_url") as string;

  const args = parseQuotedArgs(text.trim());
  if (args.length < 2) {
    return new Response(
      '❌ Invalid format. Use:
• `/create test Name Email`
• `/create ach Name Email "AccountHolder" RoutingNumber AccountNumber AccountType HolderType "Street" "City" State ZIP`
• `/create crypto Name Email WalletAddress Blockchain`'
    );
  }

  const payeeType = args[0].toLowerCase();
  let isValid = false;
  let errorMessage = "";

  if (payeeType === "test") {
    isValid = args.length >= 3;
    errorMessage = "❌ Test Rails format: `/create test Name Email`";
  } else if (payeeType === "ach") {
    isValid = args.length >= 12;
    errorMessage =
      '❌ US ACH format: `/create ach Name Email "AccountHolderName" RoutingNumber AccountNumber AccountType HolderType "Street" "City" State ZIP`';
  } else if (payeeType === "crypto") {
    isValid = args.length >= 5;
    errorMessage =
      "❌ Crypto format: `/create crypto Name Email WalletAddress Blockchain`";
  } else {
    return new Response("❌ Invalid payee type. Use: `test`, `ach`, or `crypto`");
  }

  if (!isValid) return new Response(errorMessage);

  if (payeeType === "ach") {
    const routingNumber = args[4];
    const accountType = args[6].toLowerCase();
    const holderType = args[7].toLowerCase();

    if (!/^\d{9}$/.test(routingNumber)) {
      return new Response(`❌ Routing number must be exactly 9 digits. Got: "${routingNumber}"`);
    }

    if (!["checking", "savings"].includes(accountType)) {
      return new Response("❌ Account type must be 'checking' or 'savings'");
    }

    if (!["individual", "business"].includes(holderType)) {
      return new Response("❌ Holder type must be 'individual' or 'business'");
    }
  }

  // Respond quickly to Slack
  const immediateResponse = new Response("⏳ Creating payee...");
  createPayeeInBackground(payeeType, args, responseUrl);
  return immediateResponse;
}

async function createPayeeInBackground(payeeType: string, args: string[], responseUrl: string) {
  try {
    const payman = PaymanClient.withCredentials({
      clientId: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_ID!,
      clientSecret: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_SECRET!,
    });

    const name = args[1];
    const email = args[2];

    const payeesRes = await payman.ask("list all payees");
    const payeesContent = payeesRes.artifacts?.[0]?.content || String(payeesRes);
    const existingPayees = parsePayeeNames(payeesContent);
    const existingPayee = findPayeeMatch(existingPayees, name);

    if (existingPayee) {
      return await postToSlack(responseUrl, `ℹ��� Payee "${existingPayee}" already exists.`);
    }

    let createCommand = "";

    if (payeeType === "test") {
      createCommand = `Create a new Test Rails payee named "${name}" with email "${email}"`;
    } else if (payeeType === "ach") {
      const [_, __, ___, accountHolder, routingNumber, accountNumber, accountType, holderType, street, city, state, zip] = args;
      createCommand = `Create a new US Bank Account (ACH) payee:
- Name: "${name}"
- Email: "${email}"
- Account Holder: "${accountHolder}"
- Routing: "${routingNumber}"
- Account: "${accountNumber}"
- Type: "${accountType}"
- Holder Type: "${holderType}"
- Address: "${street}, ${city}, ${state} ${zip}"`;
    } else if (payeeType === "crypto") {
      const walletAddress = args[3];
      const blockchain = args[4].toLowerCase();

      const supported = ["ethereum", "polygon", "base", "arbitrum", "avalanche", "optimism", "solana"];
      if (!supported.includes(blockchain)) throw new Error(`Unsupported blockchain: ${blockchain}`);

      createCommand = `Create a new Crypto Address payee named "${name}" with email "${email}", wallet address "${walletAddress}" on ${blockchain}`;
    }

    const createRes = await payman.ask(createCommand);
    const content = createRes.artifacts?.[0]?.content || String(createRes);

    const failed = ["wasn't able to create", "unable to create", "cannot create", "can't create", "limitation"].some(k => content.toLowerCase().includes(k));

    const message = failed
      ? `❌ Failed to create payee "${name}". Reason: ${content}`
      : `✅ Payee "${name}" created successfully (${payeeType.toUpperCase()}).

Details: ${content}`;

    await postToSlack(responseUrl, message);
  } catch (error) {
    const msg = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
    await postToSlack(responseUrl, `❌ Error creating payee: ${msg}`);
  }
}

async function postToSlack(responseUrl: string, text: string) {
  await fetch(responseUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ text, response_type: "in_channel" }),
  });
}

2. Payment Logic

app/api/slack/pay/route.ts

// app/api/slack/pay/route.ts
import { PaymanClient } from "@paymanai/payman-ts";

// Extract payee names from PaymanAI response
function parsePayeeNames(payeesContent: string): string[] {
  return payeesContent
    .split("
")
    .map(line => line.match(/^\s*(?:\d+\.|\•)\s*([^(]+?)(?:\s*\([^)]*\))?\s*$/))
    .filter(Boolean)
    .map(match => match![1].trim());
}

// Match exact payee name (case-insensitive)
function findPayeeMatch(payeeNames: string[], targetName: string): string | null {
  const target = targetName.toLowerCase().trim();
  return payeeNames.find(name => name.toLowerCase().trim() === target) || null;
}

// Attempt to extract a transaction ID from a raw text response
function extractTransactionId(paymentContent: string): string | null {
  const patterns = [
    /transaction\s+id[:\s]+([a-zA-Z0-9-_]+)/i,
    /txid[:\s]+([a-zA-Z0-9-_]+)/i,
    /tx[:\s]+([a-zA-Z0-9-_]+)/i,
    /hash[:\s]+([a-zA-Z0-9-_]+)/i,
    /id[:\s]+([a-zA-Z0-9-_]{10,})/i,
  ];

  for (const pattern of patterns) {
    const match = paymentContent.match(pattern);
    if (match) return match[1];
  }

  return null;
}

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const formData = await req.formData();
  const text = formData.get("text") as string;
  const responseUrl = formData.get("response_url") as string;

  // Define fallback regex matchers for flexible /pay command syntax
  const patterns = [
    { name: "Current", regex: /\$(\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?)\s+.*?to\s+(.+?)$/i },
    { name: "Simple", regex: /\$(\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?).*to\s+(\w+)/i },
    { name: "Flexible", regex: /\$(\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?).*to\s+(.+)/i },
    { name: "Very Flexible", regex: /\$(\d+(?:\.\d{1,2})?).*?to\s*(.+?)$/i },
  ];

  let match: RegExpMatchArray | null = null;
  let matchedPattern = null;

  for (const pattern of patterns) {
    const testMatch = text.match(pattern.regex);
    if (testMatch && !match) {
      match = testMatch;
      matchedPattern = pattern.name;
    }
  }

  if (!match) {
    return new Response(
      `❌ Invalid format. Use: /pay $100 for Uber to Ramesh or /pay $1.35 to Akash

Your command: ${JSON.stringify(text)}`
    );
  }

  const amount = match[1];
  const payeeName = match[2].trim();

  // Respond quickly to Slack
  const immediateResponse = new Response("⏳ Processing your /pay command...");
  processPaymentInBackground(amount, payeeName, responseUrl);
  return immediateResponse;
}

async function processPaymentInBackground(amount: string, payeeName: string, responseUrl: string) {
  try {
    const payman = PaymanClient.withCredentials({
      clientId: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_ID!,
      clientSecret: process.env.PAYMAN_CLIENT_SECRET!,
    });

    const payeesRes = await payman.ask("list all payees");
    const payeesContent = payeesRes.artifacts?.[0]?.content || String(payeesRes);
    const payeeNames = parsePayeeNames(payeesContent);

    const matchedPayee = findPayeeMatch(payeeNames, payeeName);
    let finalMessage = "";

    if (!matchedPayee) {
      finalMessage = `❌ Payee ${payeeName} not found. Use /create to add.`;
    } else {
      const payResponse = await payman.ask(`Send ${amount} USDC to ${matchedPayee}`);
      const paymentContent = payResponse.artifacts?.[0]?.content || String(payResponse);
      const transactionId = extractTransactionId(paymentContent);

      finalMessage = transactionId
        ? `✅ Paid $${amount} USDC to ${matchedPayee}. Transaction ID: ${transactionId}`
        : `✅ Paid $${amount} USDC to ${matchedPayee}. Payment completed successfully.`;
    }

    await postToSlack(responseUrl, finalMessage);
  } catch (error) {
    const msg = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
    await postToSlack(responseUrl, `❌ Error processing payment: ${msg}`);
  }
}

async function postToSlack(responseUrl: string, text: string) {
  await fetch(responseUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ text, response_type: "in_channel" }),
  });
}

These handle argument parsing, validation, async Slack responses, and connect with the Payman API under the hood.

/create crypto Alice alice@example.com 0x742d35... ethereum

/pay $500 to Sarah  
/pay $2500 for design work to Alice

Conclusion

The future of payments isn’t forms, dashboards, or portals.

It’s context-aware, embedded, and conversational.

Slack is just the start 🎉

title: Best AI Tools Better Than ChatGPT for Specific Tasks (2026)
subtitle: ChatGPT is the Swiss army knife of AI - decent at most things, best at none. Here are 7 specialized AI tools that beat i...
content:
ChatGPT is the Swiss army knife of AI - decent at most things, best at none. Here are 7 specialized AI tools that beat it when it actually matters, most of them flying well under the radar.

What You'll Learn

  • Which AI tools are better than ChatGPT for research, math, meetings, and presentations

  • Why specialized AI tools outperform general-purpose chatbots for specific jobs

  • Free and paid options for every use case

Why ChatGPT Isn't Always the Best AI Tool

ChatGPT is everywhere. It's the default. When someone says "I used AI for this," they almost always mean ChatGPT. But here's the thing nobody says out loud: being the most popular tool and being the best tool for a specific job are two very different things.

Every tool on this list was built to win at one specific job. And in that job, it does.

The core problem with ChatGPT:

  • It can hallucinate facts without citing sources

  • It has no memory of your meetings or calls

  • It can't search 125 million academic papers

  • It outputs bullet points, not designed presentations

1. Perplexity AI - For Research & Fact-Checking

What is Perplexity AI? Perplexity AI is an answer engine that provides every response with clickable inline citations from real, verifiable sources.

It doesn't just answer your question - it shows you exactly where it learned the answer. Built from the ground up as a research engine, not retrofitted with search. Its Academic mode filters exclusively to peer-reviewed sources, which ChatGPT's browsing feature cannot match.

Why Perplexity AI beats ChatGPT for research: Unlike ChatGPT, Perplexity cites every claim inline so you can verify facts directly. This makes it the go-to for journalists, students, and analysts who have been burned by hallucinated answers.

Best for: Fact-checking, sourced research, academic queries, news verification

Pricing: Free tier available. Pro plan for unlimited searches.

🔗 perplexity.ai

2. Elicit - For Academic Research

What is Elicit? Elicit is an AI research assistant that searches 125+ million academic papers and extracts structured data - methodology, findings, sample size - side-by-side across multiple studies.

This is not ChatGPT with a search bar. It's built for systematic reviews, and it replaces weeks of manual paper-screening. Completely underrated outside academia.

Why Elicit beats ChatGPT for academic research: ChatGPT generates summaries from training data. Elicit reads actual peer-reviewed papers and extracts real data with sentence-level citations. There's no comparison for rigorous literature reviews.

Best for: Literature reviews, systematic reviews, academic paper analysis, PhD research

Pricing: Free tier covers most use cases. Paid plans for power users.

🔗 elicit.com

3. NotebookLM - For Working With Your Own Documents

What is NotebookLM? NotebookLM is Google's AI research assistant that only answers from sources you upload - your PDFs, notes, and documents. No hallucinations from external training data.

Ask it "what did the report say about Q3 risks?" and it cites the exact sentence. The Audio Overview feature turns your documents into a podcast-style discussion - which sounds gimmicky until you use it on a 200-page report you'd never otherwise read.

Why NotebookLM beats ChatGPT for document analysis: ChatGPT can mix in information from its training data when analyzing your documents. NotebookLM is grounded only in what you upload, making every answer traceable and verifiable.

Best for: PDF analysis, contract review, research synthesis, report summarization

Pricing: Free with a Google account.

🔗 notebooklm.google.com

4. Gamma - For Presentations

What is Gamma? Gamma is an AI presentation tool that generates a complete, professionally designed slide deck from a single text prompt in under two minutes.

Gamma isn't a slide template tool - it understands structure, narrative flow, and visual hierarchy. What ChatGPT outputs as a bullet-point dump, Gamma turns into something you'd actually send to a client.

Why Gamma beats ChatGPT for presentations: ChatGPT writes content. Gamma designs slides. If the deliverable is a presentation, there is no contest - Gamma produces client-ready decks that ChatGPT simply cannot.

Best for: Business presentations, pitch decks, reports, educational slides

Pricing: Free tier available.

🔗 gamma.app

5. Otter.ai - For Meetings & Voice

What is Otter.ai? Otter.ai is an AI meeting assistant that provides real-time transcription, AI-generated summaries, and action items for every call. It integrates with Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams.

The standout feature: you can ask Otter questions about past meetings mid-conversation - "what did we decide about the budget last week?" - and it pulls the exact timestamp. No more re-watching hour-long recordings.

Why Otter.ai beats ChatGPT for meetings: ChatGPT has no memory of your calls, conversations, or decisions. Otter records, transcribes, and makes your entire meeting history searchable and queryable.

Best for: Meeting notes, action item tracking, interview transcription, team alignment

Pricing: Free tier available. Pro from $16.99/month.

🔗 otter.ai

6. Wolfram Alpha - For Math & Precise Computation

What is Wolfram Alpha? Wolfram Alpha is a computational intelligence engine that calculates exact answers to mathematical, scientific, and data queries - it does not generate or approximate.

Old but extremely underestimated in the ChatGPT era. Wolfram doesn't generate - it computes. For anything involving numbers, equations, unit conversions, statistics, or factual data (population figures, physics constants, financial formulas), it is categorically more reliable than any LLM.

Why Wolfram Alpha beats ChatGPT for math: LLMs guess. Wolfram calculates. When the answer is either right or wrong, a language model's probabilistic output is the wrong tool. Wolfram gives you the correct answer, every time.

Best for: Calculus, algebra, unit conversions, statistics, physics problems, financial calculations

Pricing: Free. Pro from $7.99/month.

🔗 wolframalpha.com

7. ResearchRabbit - For Literature Discovery

What is ResearchRabbit? ResearchRabbit is a free AI tool that maps citation networks around academic papers. Often called "Spotify for research papers" - upload a few papers you already know and it surfaces everything related: prior works, derivative studies, and adjacent research you'd never find by keyword search alone.

Completely free. Completely unknown outside academic circles. Genuinely one of the best AI-powered tools nobody is talking about.

Why ResearchRabbit beats ChatGPT for literature discovery: ChatGPT summarizes what it knows from training. ResearchRabbit maps the actual citation network of real papers, surfacing connections and foundational works that no keyword search would find.

Best for: Exploring a new research field, systematic literature mapping, finding foundational papers

Pricing: Free.

🔗 researchrabbitapp.com

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an AI better than ChatGPT? For specific tasks, yes. Perplexity beats ChatGPT for sourced research. Wolfram Alpha beats it for math. Elicit beats it for academic papers. No single tool beats ChatGPT at everything, but each of these tools beats it at one specific job.

What is the best free AI tool besides ChatGPT? NotebookLM, ResearchRabbit, and Perplexity all offer strong free tiers. For document analysis specifically, NotebookLM (free) is arguably better than ChatGPT Plus for working with your own files.

What AI tool is best for research? It depends on the research type. For sourced web research: Perplexity. For academic papers: Elicit or ResearchRabbit. For analyzing documents you already have: NotebookLM.

What is better than ChatGPT for presentations? Gamma. It generates fully designed slide decks from a prompt, not just text outlines. ChatGPT cannot design slides - Gamma was built specifically for this.

Can I use these tools for free? Most of them, yes. NotebookLM, ResearchRabbit, and basic Perplexity are completely free. Elicit, Otter.ai, and Gamma all have usable free tiers.

Quick Reference: Which AI Tool Should You Use?

Use Case Best Tool Free?
Verified facts with citations Perplexity AI Yes
Academic literature review Elicit Yes
Exploring a research field ResearchRabbit Yes
Analyzing your own documents NotebookLM Yes
Creating presentations Gamma Free tier
Meeting transcription Otter.ai Free tier
Math and computation Wolfram Alpha Yes

The bottom line

ChatGPT and its big-name cousins are excellent generalists. But "generalist" is just another word for "average at everything." The best AI setup in 2026 isn't one tool. It's knowing which one to reach for.

Quick cheat sheet:

  • Need verified facts? → Perplexity

  • Reviewing academic papers? → Elicit or ResearchRabbit

  • Analyzing your own documents? → NotebookLM

  • Making a presentation? → Gamma

  • Recapping meetings? → Otter.ai

  • Need exact math? → Wolfram Alpha

  • Exploring a new research field? → ResearchRabbit

What if the future of money belongs to... agents? Not human ones. AI ones.

And it’s going to change everything.

So what do I mean by "AI agents with money?"

I’m talking about autonomous software agents that can:

  • hold digital wallets,

  • send money (like real USDC, USD),

  • hire freelancers,

  • pay invoices,

  • or even... tip someone for a good answer in Slack (in case my team members are reading … ahem ahem 👀)

It’ll take time. But we’ll get there. And the ones who start building now will be the ones who shape how all this plays out.

TL;DR? Money is going agent-native.

In the next few years, we won’t be initiating most of our payments. Our AI agents will.

We’ll just set goals and guardrails. And they’ll handle the rest.

So yeah. The future of money isn’t human. It’s autonomous.

And I’m here for it.

content:
It’s been a while since I shared a fun project, so here’s something I whipped up over the weekend! This app is called the World Mood-O-Meter (Try It Here). The idea is really simple - we figure out the mood of a country based on real-time news. Using data fetched with SerpApi, we run sentiment analysis on the news headlines with the help of an AI model (I’m using GPT-4 via OpenRouter). If you just want to build this project without spending anything, feel free to grab any model from HuggingFace!

Important Tools

SerpApi

SerpApi is a powerful real-time API designed to fetch Google search results and data from other search engines and websites. It takes care of the heavy lifting, like managing proxies, solving CAPTCHAs, and parsing data into an organized, easy-to-use format.

With SerpApi, developers can interact directly with search engines and access structured search results that are ready for analysis or integration into applications. This makes it ideal for SEO monitoring, market research, or competitive analysis tasks. The best part? You don’t need to worry about building or maintaining complex web scraping systems—SerpApi does everything for you.

I love that I can get access to all this below information from a single place, with very easy implementation.

OpenRouter

OpenRouter is an AI platform that offers seamless access to a variety of advanced AI models from providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Using its OpenAI-compatible completion API, you can easily integrate state-of-the-art models into your projects without additional setup.

One standout feature of OpenRouter is its ability to route your requests to the best-suited AI model for your task. It also supports structured outputs, ensuring the responses are always clean and follow the required format. Whether developing AI-driven applications or exploring new AI capabilities, OpenRouter makes the integration process simple and scalable.

My favorite thing is on-demand credits top-up - so it doesn’t empty my bank!

Understanding World Mood-O-Meter

The World Mood-O-Meter pulls real-time news from the web (thanks to SerpApi’s Google News API) and uses AI-powered sentiment analysis to figure out the country’s current vibe. Is it positive, neutral, or negative?

Why Build This?

Because it’s fun!! This project combines a mix of APIs, data processing, and AI in a simple, practical way. Plus, it’s just plain cool to see real-time mood updates for different countries!

Implementation

We’re building this app using Next.js (App Router) along with TypeScript and ShadCN UI for styling. Let’s dive into each step, breaking down the files and explaining what’s happening.

1. Setting Up the Project

Start by creating your Next.js project. Open your terminal and run:

npx create-next-app@latest

When prompted, choose TypeScript and App Router to set up your app with the latest features.

Once your app is created, you'll need to add ShadCN components for reusable UI elements. Run these commands to get started:

npx shadcn@latest init
npx shadcn@latest add card                    
npx shadcn@latest add input
npx shadcn@latest add command
npx shadcn@latest add popover
npx shadcn@latest add button
npx shadcn@latest add scroll-area
npx shadcn@latest add alert
npx shadcn@latest add badge
npx shadcn@latest add skeleton

Next, install the additional dependencies for your project:

npm install react-svg-worldmap lucide-react

And that's it! Your project is now set up with all the tools you'll need to build the World Mood-O-Meter.

2. Setting Up Environment Variables

We need two API keys: one for SerpAPI (here) to fetch news and another for OpenRouter to use GPT-4 for sentiment analysis. Add these to your .env.local file (this file should be in your root folder):

# SerpAPI Key
SERPAPI_KEY=your-serpapi-key

# OpenRouter Key
NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENROUTER_KEY=your-openrouter-key

Replace your-serpapi-key and your-openrouter-key with your actual keys. These keys are essential for the app to function properly.

3. Fetch News API (app/api/news/route.ts)

This file contains the backend API route that fetches real-time news for a specific country using SerpAPI. Here’s what’s happening:

  1. Receive the Country Name: When the user selects a country on the map, the frontend sends a POST request with the country name.

  2. Fetch News: We use SerpAPI's Google News engine to fetch the latest news headlines for that country. It handles all the tricky stuff like CAPTCHA solving and parsing the data.

  3. Return Results: The API returns the news in a structured format, which the front end can easily display.

import { NextResponse } from "next/server";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
    try {
        const { country } = await request.json();

        if (!country) {
            return NextResponse.json(
                { error: "Country is required" },
                { status: 400 }
            );
        }

        const params: Record<string, string> = {
            engine: "google_news",
            q: `${country} news`,
            gl: "us",
            hl: "en",
            api_key: process.env.SERPAPI_KEY || "",
        };

        console.log("API Key available:", !!process.env.SERPAPI_KEY);

        const searchParams = new URLSearchParams(params);
        const url = `https://serpapi.com/search?${searchParams.toString()}`;

        const debugUrl = url.replace(
            process.env.SERPAPI_KEY || "",
            "[API_KEY]"
        );
        console.log("Calling URL:", debugUrl);

        const response = await fetch(url);
        console.log("SerpAPI Response Status:", response.status);

        if (!response.ok) {
            const errorText = await response.text();
            console.error("SerpAPI Error:", errorText);
            throw new Error(
                `SerpAPI returned ${response.status}: ${errorText}`
            );
        }

        const data = await response.json();

        if (!data.news_results) {
            console.log("Response data structure:", Object.keys(data));
            throw new Error("No news results in response");
        }

        return NextResponse.json({
            news_results: data.news_results,
        });
    } catch (error) {
        console.error("Detailed error:", error);
        return NextResponse.json(
            {
                error: "Error fetching news",
            },
            { status: 500 }
        );
    }
}

4. Main Page (app/page.tsx)

The main page of our app renders the MoodMap component, which displays the interactive world map. This is the entry point for users.

import MoodMap from "@/components/MoodMap";

export default function Home() {
    return (
        <main className="min-h-screen p-4">
            <MoodMap />
        </main>
    );
}

5. Mood Map Component (components/MoodMap.tsx)

This is the heart ❤️ of our app. The MoodMap component:

  • Displays the World Map: Users can click on any country.

  • Handles Search: Allows users to search for a country by name.

  • Fetches News: Calls the /api/news route to get the latest news.

  • Analyzes Sentiment: Sends the news headlines to OpenRouter to analyze the mood.

Here’s how it works:

  1. State Management: We use React state hooks to track selected country, news data, mood, and loading status.

  2. Interactive Map: The react-svg-worldmap library creates a clickable map.

  3. Fetching News: When a country is clicked, we fetch its news and analyze the mood using GPT-4.

import { Card, CardContent, CardHeader, CardTitle } from "@/components/ui/card";

const NewsSection = ({ selectedCountry, loading, mood, news, moodExplanation }: NewsSectionProps) => {
  const getMoodEmoji = (currentMood: string | null) => {
    const moods = {
      positive: "😊",

      neutral: "😐"
    };
    return moods[currentMood as keyof typeof moods] || "🤔";
  };

title: Learn to use Supabase with Next JS - A Beginner Friendly Application
subtitle: Hello, Folks! It's been a while 👀 I'm back with a straightforward tutorial that guides you through building a simple ap...
content:
Hello, Folks! It's been a while 👀

I'm back with a straightforward tutorial that guides you through building a simple application using Supabase on the backend and Next JS on the front end. This tutorial aims to help you grasp the process of easily writing and retrieving data from a database.

Technologies Used:

  1. Next JS

  2. Tailwind CSS

  3. Supabase

What are we building?

We're creating a collaborative storytelling application. In this app, anyone can contribute a new story or edit an existing one. The basic functionality includes adding a story, which in turn adds new data to the database, and editing an existing story, which updates any relevant preexisting data.

Here's the application: https://storycreator-app.vercel.app/

Let's Start

First thing first, let's set up Next JS with Supabase.

npx create-next-app@latest supabase-story-app
cd supabase-story-app
npm i @supabase/supabase-js

Launch the code editor of your choice; for this tutorial, we'll be using VS Code. Additionally, ensure that you've opted for TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and App Router during the setup process.

Supabase Setup

Next, navigate to the Supabase Dashboard. If you don't have an account, sign up, and then create a new project named story-app.

Inside the created project, go to the SQL Editor and establish a new table called stories using the following query:

CREATE TABLE stories (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT,
  content TEXT
);

This command will generate a table with columns for id, title, and content.

Awesome! Your database and table are now set up. However, you may encounter an error where Supabase returns an empty array when attempting to build the UI. This is because Supabase requires the setup of Row Level Security (RLS). Follow these steps to create one for your database:

  1. Navigate to the Authentication Tab.

  2. Click on Policies -> New Policy -> Get Started Quickly.

  3. Choose the appropriate policy; here, we use "Enable read access to everyone." Save the policy.

As we aim to display stories on our web app, let's insert one. Go to the SQL Editor tab and execute the following query:

INSERT INTO Story (title, content) VALUES ('First Story', 'This is the content of the first story.');

Fantastic! You've now configured your database, created a table, and added some data.

Now, let's dive into building the front end!

Integrate Supabase with Next JS

Before we get started, we'll need a few values to establish the connection. Navigate to the Supabase Dashboard, click on the "Project Settings" tab, and then select "API." From here, we require the Project URL and Project API Key. Copy these values and return them to your code editor.

In the root directory, create a file named .env.local and paste the values as follows:

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=Your-Project-URL
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_KEY=Your-API-Key

To ensure that the environment variables work, download the dotenv package in the terminal:

npm i dotenv

In your root folder, create a "services" folder, and inside it, create a file named supabase.ts

import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';

const supabaseUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL;
const supabaseKey = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_KEY;

// Check if Supabase URL or API Key is missing and throw an error if so
if (!supabaseUrl || !supabaseKey) {
    throw new Error('Supabase URL or API Key is missing');
}

// Create a Supabase client using the retrieved URL and API Key
export const supabase = createClient(supabaseUrl, supabaseKey);

Fantastic! You've now successfully established the connection.

Let's create another file in the services folder named "storyServices.ts" and add the following code:

// Import necessary functions and types from the Supabase JavaScript library
import {PostgrestResponse, PostgrestSingleResponse } from "@supabase/supabase-js";
import { supabase } from "./supabase";

// Define the structure of a Story using TypeScript interface
interface Story {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
} 

// Async function to fetch stories from the "stories" table in Supabase
export const getStories = async (): Promise<Story[] | null> => {
    // Make a request to select all columns from the "stories" table
    const { data, error }: PostgrestResponse<Story> = await supabase.from('stories').select('*');

    // If an error occurs during the request, throw the error
    if (error) {
        throw error;
    }

    // Return the fetched data (an array of stories) or null if there's no data
    return data;
};

// Async function to update a story's content in the "stories" table in Supabase
export const updateStory = async (
    id: number,
    newStory: Partial<Story>
): Promise<PostgrestSingleResponse<Story | null>> => {
    // Make a request to Supabase to update the content of a story based on its ID
    const { data, error, count, status, statusText } = await supabase
        .from("stories")
        .update({ content: newStory.content })
        .eq("id", id);

    // If an error occurs during the request, throw the error
    if (error) {
        throw error;
    }

    // Return an object containing the updated data (story) or null if there's no data,
    // along with other response properties such as count, status, and statusText
    return { data: data as Story | null, error, count, status, statusText };
};

Great! The main services are now updated. Let's move on to the UI!

Creating Frontend

Create a "components" folder in the root directory; this folder will contain all the components required for our web app.

Disclaimer: The app uses Tailwind CSS for UI. I won't delve into its details to keep the article simple.

In the "components" folder, create a "Story.tsx" file and add the following code:

"use client"
// Import the necessary modules and define the interface for the Story component
import React, { ChangeEvent, useState } from "react";

// Define the props for the Story component
interface StoryProps {
  story: {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
  };
  onEdit: (editedStory: {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
  }) => void;
}

// Define the Story component as a functional component
const Story: React.FC<StoryProps> = ({ story, onEdit }) => {
  // State to manage the edited story and editing status
  const [editedStory, setEditedStory] = useState(story);
  const [isEditing, setIsEditing] = useState(false);

  // Function to handle saving edits
  const handleEdit = () => {
    onEdit(editedStory);
    setIsEditing(false); // Reset editing state after saving
  };

  // Function to handle changes in the content textarea
  const handleContentChange = (e: ChangeEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>) => {
    setEditedStory({ ...editedStory, content: e.target.value });
  };

  // Return the JSX structure of the Story component
  return (
    <div className={`relative bg-gray-100 bg-opacity-${isEditing ? '75' : '50'} p-6 rounded-lg overflow-hidden shadow-xl transition-all duration-300 hover:bg-blur mx-4 mt-8`}>
      <div className="relative z-10 text-black">
        <div className="mb-4">
          {/* Display the title with different font sizes for different screen sizes */}
          <h2 className="font-bold text-xl md:text-2xl lg:text-3xl mb-2">{story.title}</h2>

          {/* Display the content paragraph without a background only when not editing */}
          {!isEditing && (
            <p className="font-light text-gray-800 text-base md:text-lg lg:text-xl overflow-hidden overflow-ellipsis whitespace-nowrap">
              {story.content}
            </p>
          )}
        </div>

        {/* Display textarea and button only when editing */}
        {isEditing && (
          <>
            <textarea
              className="resize-none border rounded-md p-2 mb-4 w-full h-40 md:h-48 lg:h-56 focus:ring-4"
              value={editedStory.content}
              onChange={handleContentChange}
              placeholder="Type your story here..."
            />
            <button className="bg-gray-700 hover:bg-gray-900 text-white font-normal py-2 px-6 rounded-full transition duration-300" onClick={handleEdit}>
              Save Edit
            </button>
          </>
        )}

        {/* Button to trigger editing */}
        {!isEditing && (
          <button className="bg-gray-700 hover:bg-gray-900 text-white font-normal py-2 px-6 rounded-full transition duration-300" onClick={() => setIsEditing(true)}>
            Continue...
          </button>
        )}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

// Export the Story component as the default export of the file
export default Story;

Now, to display all these story cards in a responsive grid on our web app, create a "StoryList.tsx" file in the "components" folder and add the following code:

// Import React and the Story component
"use client"
import React from "react";
import Story from "./Story";

// Define the props for the StoryList component
interface StoryListProps {
  stories: {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
  }[];
  onEdit: (
    editedStory: {
      id: number;
      title: string;
      content: string;
    }
  ) => void;
}

// Define the StoryList component as a functional component
const StoryList: React.FC<StoryListProps> = ({ stories, onEdit }) => {
  return (
    <>
      {/* Display a title for the list of stories */}
      <h1 className="text-center font-bold text-3xl sm:text-4xl md:text-5xl mt-8 text-purple-500">
        List Of Stories
      </h1>

      {/* Display a grid of stories using the Story component */}
      <div className="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-4">
        {/* Map through the stories array and render a Story component for each story */}
        {stories.map((story) => (
          <Story key={story.id} story={story} onEdit={onEdit} />
        ))}
      </div>
    </>
  );
};

// Export the StoryList component as the default export of the file
export default StoryList;

Let's create a form component that facilitates the addition of a new story to the database. In the components folder create an AddStory.tsx file

"use client"
import React, { useState } from "react";
import { supabase } from "../services/supabase";

// Define the props for the AddStory component
interface AddStoryFormProps {
  onAdd: () => void; // Callback function to be executed after adding a story
}

const AddStory: React.FC<AddStoryFormProps> = ({ onAdd }) => {
  // State to manage the title and content input values
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [content, setContent] = useState("");

  // Function to handle adding a new story to the database
  const handleAddStory = async () => {
    try {
      // Check if both title and content are provided
      if (title && content) {
        // Make a request to add or update a story in the "stories" table
        const { data, error } = await supabase
          .from("stories")
          .upsert([{ title, content }]);

        if (error) {
          throw error; // Throw an error if the request encounters an issue
        }

        // Clear the form and trigger the parent component to refresh the story list
        setTitle("");
        setContent("");
        onAdd(); // Execute the callback function passed as a prop
      }
    } catch (error: any) {
      console.error("Error adding story:", error.message);
    }
  };

  // JSX structure for the form component
  return (
    <div className="m-6 flex items-center justify-center">
      {/* Set full prop to make it cover the entire page */}
      <div className="bg-white rounded-md p-8">
        <h2 className="text-black text-2xl font-bold mb-4">Add New Story</h2>
        <form>
          {/* Title input field */}
          <label className="text-black mb-4 block">
            Title:
            <input
              className="border rounded-md p-2 w-full"
              type="text"
              value={title}
              onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)}
            />
          </label>
          {/* Content textarea */}
          <label className=" text-black mb-4 block">
            Content:
            <textarea
              className="border rounded-md p-2 w-full"
              value={content}
              onChange={(e) => setContent(e.target.value)}
            />
          </label>
          {/* Button to trigger the handleAddStory function */}
          <button
            className="bg-purple-500 text-white font-semibold rounded-md py-2 px-4"
            type="button"
            onClick={handleAddStory}
          >
            Add Story
          </button>
        </form>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

export default AddStory;

Now best the part, add the components on a page.tsx file under the app directory.

"use client"
import { getStories, updateStory } from "@/services/storyServices"; // Import functions for fetching and updating stories
import React, { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import AddStory from "@/components/AddStory"; // Import the AddStory component
import StoryList from "@/components/StoryList"; // Import the StoryList component

// Define the Home component as a functional component
const Home: React.FC = () => {
  // State to manage the list of stories
  const [stories, setStories] = useState<{
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
  }[]>([]);

  // useEffect hook to fetch stories when the component mounts
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchStories();
  }, []);

  // Function to fetch stories from the database
  const fetchStories = async () => {
    try {
      // Make a request to get stories using the getStories function
      const storiesData = await getStories();
      // Update the state with the fetched stories (or an empty array if there's an error)
      setStories(storiesData || []);
    } catch (error: any) {
      console.error("Fetched Error: ", error.message);
    }
  };

  // Function to handle adding a new story
  const handleAdd = () => {
    // Refresh the story list after adding a new story
    fetchStories();
  };

  // Function to handle editing an existing story
  const handleEdit = async (editedStory: {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    content: string;
  }) => {
    // Update the state with the edited story
    const updatedStories = stories.map((s) => (s.id === editedStory.id ? editedStory : s));
    setStories(updatedStories);

    try {
      // Make a request to update the story using the updateStory function
      await updateStory(editedStory.id, editedStory);
    } catch (error: any) {
      console.error("Error updating story:", error.message);
    }
  };

  // JSX structure for the Home component
  return (
    <div className="flex flex-col min-h-screen">
      {/* AddStory component for adding new stories */}
      <AddStory onAdd={handleAdd} />
      {/* StoryList component for displaying the list of stories */}
      <StoryList stories={stories} onEdit={handleEdit} />
      {/* Footer section */}
      <footer className="mt-20 py-4 text-center text-black font-semibold">
        Made with <span className="text-pink-500">♥</span> by Vanshika
      </footer>
    </div>
  );
};

// Export the Home component as the default export of the file
export default Home;

title: How to Send Emails in Node JS using the SendGrid API
subtitle: Emails are an essential element of any business's communication; as more organizations establish an online presence, it...
content:
Emails are an essential element of any business's communication; as more organizations establish an online presence, it becomes increasingly crucial for them to maintain effective contact with their consumers and staff; nevertheless, performing this activity manually may be time-consuming.

Twilio's SendGrid enables businesses to meet this demand by providing a CRM that is adaptable and extremely efficient.

In this article, we'll look at how to send emails in Node JS using the SendGrid API.

Prerequisites

You'll need

  • Node.js: Make sure you have node. js version 14.6.1 or higher installed in your system.
  • Text Editor: For this article, I'll be using VSCode, but you are free to use any editor of your choice.
  • SendGrid Account: If you are new you can sign up or if you already have an account just login.

Getting Started with SendGrid

Following the successful creation of your account, you will be led to the SendGrid dashboard. On the left sidebar, you'll find a lot of categories, but for now, we are only interested in the Sender Authentication under the settings dropdown menu and Email API.

Sender Authentication

The first step is to authenticate the sender from whom the email will be sent. If you are a new user, you will be asked to verify the sender when you log in.

  • Navigate to the left panel and click the settings dropdown menu to select Sender Authentication.

  • After selecting, you'll be directed to this page.

There are two types of authentication Domain Authentication and Single Sender Verification.

Domain Authentication allows all email addresses linked with your domain to send emails, whereas Single Sender Verification only allows one email address to send emails.

  • For the time being, we'll only be authenticating one user, so click the "Verify a Single Sender" button. You will be sent to the following page. Fill out all of the required information and create the verified account.

Email API

  • Now, we'll get the Email API key to integrate SendGrid with our Node JS. From the left panel select Email API and then Integration Guide.

  • You'll be sent to a page similar to this one. Select "Web API" now.

  • Choose Node.js

  • Give a name to your API key and click "Create Key"

  • Copy the key and keep it somewhere safe.

Integrating with Node JS

Now that we've got our API key, we'll get to work on integrating it with Node JS.

  • Make a new folder and open it in VSCode (or any other editor).
  • Open the terminal, run the following and follow the instructions:
npm init

This will set up an npm project.

  • Run the following commands in your terminal to configure environment variables.

Replace "YOUR_API_KEY" with the key you copied above.

echo "export SENDGRID_API_KEY='YOUR_API_KEY'" > sendgrid.env
echo "sendgrid.env" >> .gitignore
source ./sendgrid.env
  • Now, using npm, install the SendGrid package.
npm install --save @sendgrid/mail
  • Create an index.js file. This will include the code for sending emails using SendGrid.

First, we'll import the API key from the .env file into the index. js

const sgMail = require('@sendgrid/mail')
sgMail.setApiKey(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY)

Now we'll write the message that will be delivered by email. This message includes the recipient's address, the sender's address, the subject, and the body. It can also contain custom HTML to style the content.

const msg = {
  to: 'test@example.com', // Recipients email address
  from: 'test@example.com', // Verified Sender: The email address that we verified in the preceding section.
  subject: 'Sending with SendGrid is Fun',
  text: 'Hey! How are you doing?', // Either text or html should be used
  html: '<strong>Hey! How are you doing?</strong>',
}

We can also send an email to several users at the same time by using arrays.

...
to: ['test@example.com', 'test2@example.com', ' test3@example.com']// List of recipients addresses
...

Another change we may make is to include the Sender's name. This name will be displayed to recipients when they get the email.

...
from: {
    name: 'THIS IS MY NAME',
    email:'test@example.com'
},
...

Finally, we'll use the send() function to send the email using the SendGrid API.

sgMail
  .send(msg)
  .then(() => {
    console.log('Email sent successfully ... ')
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error)
  })

The index.js file should look something like this.

const sgMail = require('@sendgrid/mail')
sgMail.setApiKey(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY)
const msg = {
  to: ['test@example.com', 'test2@example.com', ' test3@example.com'],
  from: {
    name: 'THIS IS MY NAME',
    email:'test@example.com'
},
  subject: 'Sending with SendGrid is Fun',
  html: '<strong>Hey! How are you doing?</strong>',

};
sgMail
  .send(msg)
  .then(() => {
    console.log('Email sent successfully ...')
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error)
  })

Let's Send the Email

Now that we have integrated Node JS and SendGrid, we will execute our code. In the terminal, run the following command:

node index.js

Check the email address to which you sent the message!

Conclusion

Hope you liked this tutorial and had fun integrating email services in your Node JS project. SendGrid is a very adaptable and powerful platform with numerous modifications and possibilities. You can check them out by heading over to SendGrid docs.
